name: Dopamine beauty

lead: Dopamine beauty carries the "dopamine dressing" idea into makeup: wearing bright colors, bold eyeshadow, vivid lips or playful finishes because they make the wearer feel happier, more confident and more visible. The appearance payoff is a livelier, more colorful look, and proponents add that feeling good shows in posture and expression.

The parent idea, dopamine dressing, was named by fashion psychologist Dawnn Karen. Researchers who study clothing and mind, such as Adam and Galinsky's enclothed cognition work, have reported effects of worn garments on thinking, though several replications have failed. Makeup-specific research is thin.

paras: In practice people choose saturated colors that they personally associate with good moods, such as bright lids, colorful liner, vivid lipstick or blush, often matched with bright clothing. Karen stresses that colors affect people differently, so the choice is personal.
Cosmetics carry ordinary risks such as irritation or allergy to specific products; the mood benefit is individual and not guaranteed.

lead: Dopamine beauty is a term for bold, colorful makeup and grooming chosen for how it feels rather than to follow a neutral "natural" standard. It borrows from dopamine dressing, a phrase coined by fashion psychologist Dr. Dawnn Karen in her book Dress Your Best Life, where it describes wearing clothes with colors and textures that lift mood.[1]

The core premise, as reported in coverage, is that bright colors and fun outfits can trigger a feel-good response, and that the wearer should find which colors and garments are personally meaningful.[1] Applied to cosmetics, it means picking vivid shades for the eyes, lips and cheeks as part of the same mood-led approach. The parent trend has been associated with TikTok and Pinterest.[1]

Psychologists quoted in coverage connect the idea to dopamine's role in motivation, but the cited articles name no studies showing that dressing improves mood.[1] Research on the related idea of enclothed cognition has had mixed replication.
infobox: Dopamine dressing, coined by Dr. Dawnn Karen [1]
Color and style chosen to enhance mood

paras: Dr. Dawnn Karen, a fashion psychologist," coined "dopamine dressing" in Dress Your Best Life, also calling it mood enhancement dressing.[1] She links the trend's rise to the pandemic, saying people gave themselves permission to choose styles that made them happy.[1]
Dopamine beauty extends the concept to makeup. Coverage of the parent idea is mainly about clothing, and the makeup version is mostly discussed as trend commentary.

Karen says bright colors such as yellow tend to create positive feelings, and that colors, patterns and textures evoke different emotions in different people.[1] Behavioral psychologist Dr. Carolyn Mair connects the idea to dopamine's role in motivation and says it is about choosing items that lead to feeling more confident, competent or happy.[1]

Related experimental work by Hajo Adam and Adam Galinsky (2012) found that participants wearing a lab coat made fewer errors on an attention task, interpreted as an effect of a garment's physical presence and symbolic meaning. Several replications, including a 2019 preregistered one, did not reproduce the effect, and a 2023 meta-analysis concluded evidential value can be affirmed for studies after 2015.[2]
No studies found on dopamine beauty or makeup itself. Related experimental research on how clothing affects wearers (enclothed cognition) is described above.[2]

timeline.event: Adam and Galinsky publish lab-coat enclothed cognition studies.[2]
